# 8. Libraries and namespaces

<!-- Generated by tools/generate-docs.lisp from docs/manual/chapters.lisp,
     docs/manual/introduction.md and the examples: do not edit by hand. -->

A library exports some of its names and keeps the rest; each file chooses how
to bring them in: unqualified, under a prefix, or a few under other names. Names
from different libraries never collide, and a full name such as shapes:area
always works.

## Libraries: what a library exports, and bringing it in

A library is a file whose first form is (library name (export ...)). Its
definitions belong to it: in shapes.lisp beside this file, (define (area w h)
...) defines shapes:area, its full name. (require "shapes.lisp") loads the
file once and brings every exported name into this file, unqualified, so
area means shapes:area here. A full name works from anywhere, imported or not.
(require 'name) finds a library on the library path instead, as
(require 'cl) does; a file name, as here, is looked for beside this file.

(imports) lists what this file brought in: each name with the full name it
stands for.

`examples/namespaces/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "shapes.lisp")

(display (area 3 4)) (newline)              ; shapes:area, through the import
(display (shapes:area 3 4)) (newline)       ; the full name: always works
(display (perimeter 3 4)) (newline)
(display (imports)) (newline)
```

`examples/namespaces/shapes.lisp`:

```scheme
(library shapes (export area perimeter))

(define (area w h) (* w h))
(define (perimeter w h) (* 2 (+ w h)))
```

Its output:

```text
12
12
14
((area . shapes:area) (perimeter . shapes:perimeter))
```

## Two libraries with the same name in them

text.lisp and engine.lisp both export a rule: text's draws a line, engine's
makes an inference rule. Without namespaces the one loaded last would replace
the other for everyone. Here each is its library's own (text:rule and
engine:rule), and this file chooses how to see them: text's unqualified, and
engine's through a prefix, (require "engine.lisp" 'prefix 'en:), which brings
every export in as en: followed by its name. The prefix is this file's choice;
another file can pick another, or none.

This program then defines a rule of its own, under another name it chose.
Defining rule itself would be an error, since this file imported text's rule
under that name (see namespaces-conflicts).

`examples/namespaces-prefix/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "text.lisp")
(require "engine.lisp" 'prefix 'en:)

(display (rule 10)) (newline)                          ; text:rule
(display (en:rule '(mortal ?x) '(man ?x))) (newline)   ; engine:rule
(display (text:rule 3)) (newline)                      ; full names work too
(display (engine:rule '(a) '(b))) (newline)

(define (house-rule n) (string-append "house " (number->string n)))
(display (house-rule 1)) (newline)
```

`examples/namespaces-prefix/engine.lisp`:

```scheme
(library engine (export rule))

(define (rule head . body) (list 'if body 'then head))
```

`examples/namespaces-prefix/text.lisp`:

```scheme
(library text (export rule))

(define (rule n) (make-string n #\-))
```

Its output:

```text
----------
(if ((man ?x)) then (mortal ?x))
---
(if ((b)) then (a))
house 1
```

## Choosing what to import: only, except, rename

require takes options, after the library's name, applied in this order:
  'only '(name ...)        just these exports;
  'except '(name ...)      every export but these;
  'rename '((old new) ...) these under other names;
  'prefix p                every one as p followed by its name.
They combine: below, palette.lisp's exports come in three times, each a
different way, under names that cannot collide. A name the library does not
export is an error in any of them, so a typo is caught at the require.

`examples/namespaces-choose/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "palette.lisp" 'only '(red green))
(require "palette.lisp" 'except '(red green blue) 'prefix 'p:)
(require "palette.lisp" 'only '(blue) 'rename '((blue sky)))

(display (list (red) (green))) (newline)          ; only
(display (list (p:mix 'red 'blue) (p:all))) (newline)  ; except, prefixed
(display (sky)) (newline)                          ; renamed
(display (palette:blue)) (newline)                 ; the full name is still there
(display (map car (imports))) (newline)

(display (guard (e (#t (error-object-message e)))
           (require "palette.lisp" 'only '(purple))))
(newline)
```

`examples/namespaces-choose/palette.lisp`:

```scheme
(library palette (export red green blue mix all))

(define (red) "#ff0000")
(define (green) "#00ff00")
(define (blue) "#0000ff")
(define (mix a b) (list 'mix a b))
(define (all) '(red green blue))
```

Its output:

```text
(#ff0000 #00ff00)
((mix red blue) (red green blue))
#0000ff
#0000ff
(green p:all p:mix red sky)
require: palette does not export purple (in only)
```

## What a library keeps to itself

counter.lisp exports next! and a macro, but not its state (count) or its
helper (%label). An import never brings in a name that is not exported, so
here count means nothing and the program cannot depend on it by accident.
A private name still has a full name, counter:count, which works from
anywhere: for a test, a debugger, or a macro that needs it. Privacy is about
what an import brings in, not a lock.

The library's macros show the two kinds. tally is hygienic (syntax-rules): its
template calls the private %label, and the expansion means counter's %label
even here, where %label is not imported. note is a define-macro, which is
not hygienic: its expansion is plain symbols, read in the file where the
macro is used, so it names the helper by its full name, counter:%label.

`examples/namespaces-private/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "counter.lisp")

(next!) (next!)
(display (next!)) (newline)                       ; 3: counter's count, through next!
(display (tally 'apples)) (newline)               ; hygienic: uses the private %label
(display (note 'pears)) (newline)                 ; define-macro: writes counter:%label

(display (guard (e (#t (error-object-message e))) count)) (newline)
(display counter:count) (newline)                 ; the full name reaches it
(display (counter:%label 'x)) (newline)
```

`examples/namespaces-private/counter.lisp`:

```scheme
(library counter (export next! tally note))

(define count 0)                                  ; private: not exported
(define (%label x) (string-append "<" (symbol->string x) ">"))

(define (next!) (set! count (+ count 1)) count)

;; hygienic: the template's %label means this library's, wherever tally is used
(define-syntax tally
  (syntax-rules ()
    ((_ what) (string-append (%label what) " counted " (number->string count)))))

;; not hygienic: the expansion is read where note is used, so it names the
;; helper in full
(define-macro (note what)
  `(string-append "note " (counter:%label ,what)))
```

Its output:

```text
3
<apples> counted 3
note <pears>
unbound variable: count
3
<x>
```

## An import belongs to the file that makes it

Each file has its own imports, as each C# file has its own using lines.
  - report.lisp is a program file that this one loads with load: it starts
    with this file's imports, as if its text were written here, so it can use
    the stats library's mean without requiring it again.
  - words.lisp is a library: a library starts with no imports at all, so it
    requires what it needs itself, here Common Lisp's names (cl), for first.
    Its import is its own: this file did not require cl, so first means
    nothing here, and words.lisp's import did not leak out.

`examples/namespaces-files/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "stats.lisp")
(load "report.lisp")
(require "words.lisp")

(display (mean '(1 2 3 6))) (newline)
(display (report '(2 4))) (newline)          ; report.lisp used this file's mean
(display (first-word "namespaces keep names apart")) (newline)
(display (guard (e (#t (error-object-message e))) (first '(a b)))) (newline)
```

`examples/namespaces-files/report.lisp`:

```scheme
(define (report xs) (string-append "mean " (number->string (mean xs))))
```

`examples/namespaces-files/stats.lisp`:

```scheme
(library stats (export mean))

(define (mean xs) (/ (apply + xs) (length xs)))
```

`examples/namespaces-files/words.lisp`:

```scheme
(library words (export first-word))
(require 'cl)                              ; this library's import, not its loader's

(define (first-word s) (first (string-split s #\space)))
```

Its output:

```text
3
mean 3
namespaces
unbound variable: first
```

## What is refused, instead of silently replaced

With one namespace, the definition loaded last wins without a word. Here a
clash is an error at the line that would cause it:
  - two imports that bring the same name into one file, from different
    libraries (left.lisp and right.lisp both export side);
  - a file defining a name it imported;
  - asking a library for a name it does not export.
The way out is always the same: a prefix, a rename, or only. (Each error is
caught here so the program can show it; eval makes the definition at run
time, so that its error can be caught too.)

One more case is a warning rather than an error, written to stderr: a program
that defines a name cog-lisp itself defines, such as http-request. The
program's own code then calls its definition, and cog-lisp's built-ins keep
calling theirs, so http-get still works.

`examples/namespaces-conflicts/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(require "left.lisp")

(define (attempt thunk)
  (display (guard (e (#t (error-object-message e))) (thunk)))
  (newline))

(attempt (lambda () (require "right.lisp")))
(attempt (lambda () (eval '(define (side) 'mine))))
(attempt (lambda () (require "right.lisp" 'only '(top))))

(require "right.lisp" 'rename '((side right-side)))
(display (list (side) (right-side))) (newline)
```

`examples/namespaces-conflicts/left.lisp`:

```scheme
(library left (export side))

(define (side) 'left)
```

`examples/namespaces-conflicts/right.lisp`:

```scheme
(library right (export side))

(define (side) 'right)
```

Its output:

```text
require: side is already imported as left:side; import one of them with a prefix, or rename it
side is imported (as left:side): choose another name, or import it with a prefix or under another name
require: right does not export top (in only)
(left right)
```
